stem: Under the Business Analysis Standard, who can be considered to be performing business analysis work?
options: Anyone performing BA activities, regardless of job title
Just staff whose title formally includes 'analyst'
Just employees in a centralized, dedicated BA department
Just individuals holding a formal IIBA certification
explanation: Business analysis is defined by the activity performed, not by job title, department, or certification — all three distractors substitute a formal marker for the actual practice.

stem: A team is deciding between a heavily documented, sequential approach and a lightweight, iterative approach for a new initiative. What should primarily drive this choice?
options: Whichever approach the analyst used most recently
The approach the loudest stakeholder happens to prefer
The initiative's complexity, risk, and stakeholder needs
Whichever approach needs the least documentation
explanation: Approach selection should be driven by the initiative's own characteristics — complexity, risk, stakeholder needs, context — not by habit, stakeholder volume, or a blanket preference for less paperwork.

stem: Which of the following is an organizational consideration that can meaningfully influence business analysis work?
options: The font style used in requirements documents
Governance structure and where decision authority sits
The color scheme of a project's presentation slides
The brand of software installed on team laptops
explanation: Governance and decision-making authority are core organizational considerations; document formatting, slide aesthetics, and hardware brand have no bearing on how BA work should be conducted.

stem: Which statement best distinguishes a requirement from a design?
options: A design is written before any requirement is captured
A requirement states the need; a design states how that need will be met
Requirements and designs are simply two names for the same artifact
Designs belong to Agile initiatives; requirements belong to Waterfall
explanation: A requirement expresses the underlying need (the 'what'); a design specifies a particular way to satisfy it (the 'how'). Sequencing myths, treating them as identical, or tying them to a specific methodology all misstate the distinction.

stem: A product owner on an agile team spends much of their time eliciting stakeholder needs and prioritizing the backlog. Under the Business Analysis Standard, is this person performing business analysis?
options: No — that description applies to people with 'analyst' in their title
No, product owners are barred from doing business analysis work
Yes, but not until the product owner earns an IIBA certification
Yes — the activity performed matches the definition of BA, regardless of title
explanation: Business analysis is defined by the work performed — eliciting needs and prioritizing them — not by holding an 'analyst' title, being barred by role, or requiring certification first.

stem: Why does the Business Analysis Standard avoid prescribing one 'correct' business analysis approach for every initiative?
options: Because the BABOK Guide has not defined any approaches to choose from
Because approaches apply mainly to IT-related initiatives
Because the right approach depends on complexity, culture, and stakeholder needs
Because IIBA discontinued the concept of an 'approach'
explanation: The right BA approach is context-dependent, shaped by complexity, culture, and stakeholder needs — it isn't that approaches are undefined, IT-only, or no longer a valid concept.

stem: An analyst rolls out a new requirements sign-off process without accounting for the organization's existing approval hierarchy. What is the most likely result?
options: No effect at all, since process design is independent of org structure
Friction or resistance, since a real organizational consideration was ignored
Immediate, automatic approval regardless of the existing hierarchy
The organization restructures itself to match the new process
explanation: Ignoring an existing governance and approval structure — a key organizational consideration — commonly creates friction and slows adoption; it doesn't disappear, guarantee approval, or trigger a restructure.

stem: A stakeholder says, 'The system must calculate shipping costs automatically.' A vendor later proposes a specific pricing algorithm and screen layout to accomplish this. How should each statement be labeled?
options: Both statements are requirements at different stages of detail
Both statements are designs, just written by different people
The stakeholder's statement is a design; the vendor's is the requirement
The stakeholder's statement is the requirement; the vendor's proposal is the design
explanation: The stakeholder's stated need is the requirement (what); the vendor's specific algorithm and layout is the design (how) — reversing the two, or collapsing them into one category, misreads the distinction.

stem: An organization eliminates its formal 'Business Analyst' job title during a restructuring, redistributing elicitation and requirements work among product owners, developers, and project managers. What does this most accurately illustrate?
options: The role's title changed, but the underlying BA discipline continues
Business analysis has effectively ended at the organization
The redistributed staff are now project managers, not analysts
The organization violated the Standard by removing the title
explanation: Business analysis is defined by the activities performed, not a specific title — when a title is retired, the practice typically persists under other roles. It hasn't ended, the staff aren't automatically relabeled PMs, and the Standard doesn't mandate that any specific title exist.

stem: A heavily regulated financial institution is weighing an agile approach against a traditional, heavily documented approach for a compliance-driven initiative. Which factor should weigh most heavily?
options: Regulatory demands for documentation and audit trails
Whichever approach is currently trending in the industry
The analyst's personal familiarity with agile ceremonies
The number of team members currently available
explanation: For a compliance-driven initiative, regulatory documentation and traceability needs should weigh most heavily — industry trends, personal familiarity, and headcount are secondary to that constraint.

stem: Which best describes how organizational culture can affect business analysis work?
options: It has no real bearing on how BA work should be conducted
It matters mainly for initiatives tied to human resources
It is fixed and cannot be factored into an analyst's approach
It shapes how stakeholders engage and how change is received
explanation: Culture influences stakeholder engagement, decision-making, and receptiveness to change — it isn't irrelevant, HR-specific, or a fixed constraint outside the analyst's consideration.

stem: How do requirements and designs typically evolve over the course of an initiative?
options: Requirements are fixed at the outset; designs alone get refined
Both are refined iteratively as requirements stabilize and designs gain detail
Designs get finalized before any requirement exists
Neither requirements nor designs change once documented
explanation: Requirements and designs both typically evolve iteratively, with designs becoming more detailed as requirements stabilize — treating either as frozen from the start, or claiming design always precedes requirements, misstates the relationship.

stem: An IT manager occasionally elicits stakeholder input and documents requirements alongside their regular technical duties. How should this be understood?
options: This isn't real business analysis since it isn't their primary role
This becomes valid once IIBA formally certifies the manager
This situation is prohibited by the Business Analysis Standard
The manager is performing BA activities as part of a blended role, which is common
explanation: Blended roles that combine BA activities with other duties are common and consistent with how responsibilities vary across organizations — the Standard neither restricts BA to primary-role holders nor requires certification to count.

stem: A team delivers using Scrum sprints, yet the business analyst produces a detailed, sign-off requirements package upfront to satisfy a regulatory reviewer before any sprint begins. What does this best illustrate?
options: The team isn't really practicing Scrum, since agile forbids upfront documentation
The analyst is violating the Standard by working outside the sprint cadence
BA approach and delivery methodology are related but distinct, not locked together
Regulatory reviewers require organizations to abandon agile delivery
explanation: BA approach (how analysis work is structured — predictive vs. adaptive) and delivery methodology (Scrum, Waterfall, etc.) are related but separable; a regulator-driven need for upfront documentation doesn't mean the team has abandoned Scrum, broken the Standard, or that agile and regulation are incompatible.

stem: An analyst joins an organization where decisions are typically made through informal hallway conversations rather than documented approvals. What is the most appropriate response?
options: Adapt the engagement approach while still capturing key decisions
Insist the organization adopt formal documented approvals immediately
Proceed exactly as done at the previous, more formal organization
Decline to work within an informal decision-making culture
explanation: Adapting to organizational context while still safeguarding critical decision capture is the sound response — demanding formal process, ignoring the culture, or refusing to engage are all poor fits.

stem: A requirement states, 'Users must reset a forgotten password.' During technical design, the team discovers the proposed emailed-link approach cannot meet a security policy, prompting the requirement to be revised to specify multi-factor verification. What does this scenario best illustrate?
options: Design decisions cannot influence a requirement once it is documented
Design work can surface constraints that feed back into refining the requirement itself
The original requirement was invalid and should be discarded outright
Security policies operate independently of both requirements and designs
explanation: Requirements and designs can inform each other iteratively — a design constraint surfacing here appropriately triggers a requirement refinement, rather than being off-limits, invalidating the original requirement outright, or treating policy as disconnected from both.

stem: Which best captures why understanding role variation matters for a foundational-level BA professional?
options: It doesn't matter, since roles are standardized everywhere
It matters mainly to hiring managers filling open roles
It helps spot others doing BA-related work, aiding collaboration
It removes the need to learn any BA techniques at all
explanation: Recognizing that BA activities can be performed under many titles helps an analyst identify collaborators doing related work — role variation doesn't mean roles are standardized, isn't only an HR concern, and doesn't substitute for learning techniques.

stem: Which best reflects a mature process for selecting a business analysis approach for a new initiative?
options: Weighing complexity, risk, and stakeholder needs before choosing an approach
Defaulting to the same approach used on every past initiative
Letting whichever stakeholder is most vocal decide the approach
Skipping an explicit approach decision and improvising as needed
explanation: A mature approach-selection process weighs complexity, risk, stakeholder needs, and culture — defaulting by habit, deferring to the loudest voice, or skipping the decision altogether all bypass that assessment.
